---
title: "Deep Learning-based Neural Granger Causality for Solar Radiation Data"
---

::: {.project-meta}
Poster · Korean Statistical Society Summer Conference 2025 · June 2025, Gyeongju · Faculty-led short-term project, Department of Statistics, Jeonbuk National University
:::

Classical Granger causality tests rest on a linear vector autoregression, which
limits what they can detect in meteorological series where the relationships are
not linear. This project applied neural Granger causality, following Tank et al.
(2021), to ask which meteorological variables carry predictive information about
solar radiation, and whether the neural formulation recovers relationships the
linear test misses.

## Data

Hourly observations for Jeonju over the whole of 2023 (8,760 records) from the
Korea Automated Synoptic Observing System: precipitation, temperature, humidity,
solar radiation, wind speed and total cloud cover.

## Methods

Component-wise MLP and component-wise LSTM models, which fit an independent
network per output variable and read Granger non-causality off the first-layer
weights under a sparsity penalty — sparse group lasso for the cMLP, group lasso
for the cLSTM. A linear VAR at the 0.005 level served as the baseline. Inputs
were min-max scaled, a lag of *k* = 12 was used, and the procedure was repeated
over 50 bootstrap samples so that each candidate relationship could be summarized
by how often it was detected.

## Findings

| Predictor of solar radiation | VAR | cMLP | cLSTM |
|---|---|---|---|
| Temperature | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| Humidity | 0.74 | 0.93 | 1.00 |
| Wind speed | 0.74 | 0.72 | 0.97 |
| Cloud cover | 0.60 | 0.65 | 0.79 |
| Precipitation | 0.37 | 0.79 | 0.97 |

: Proportion of 50 replications in which each variable was identified as a Granger cause of solar radiation {.striped}

Temperature was identified in every replication by all three methods, and
humidity was the next most consistent. The methods diverged on the variables that
behave less like continuous measurements: precipitation was detected in 37% of
replications by the VAR but 79% and 97% by the cMLP and cLSTM, and cloud cover
showed the same ordering. The neural models therefore appear better suited to
nonlinear structure in continuous variables, but the results come from a single
lag setting and these models are sensitive to hyperparameters, so their
robustness is not established.
